question: What is the range of mesosphere?
solution:
The correct answer is __**50 - 80 km**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• The mesosphere extends from approximately **50 to 80 kilometers (31 to 50 miles) above the Earth's surface**.

• It is the third layer of the Earth's atmosphere, located above the stratosphere and below the thermosphere.

• This layer is characterized by a decrease in temperature with height, making it the coldest layer of the atmosphere.

• Meteors burn up in the mesosphere due to the high level of friction with the air particles in this layer.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Atmospheric Layers:**

• **Troposphere:** The lowest layer of the atmosphere, extending up to about 8-15 km (5-9 miles) above sea level. It is where most of the Earth's weather occurs.

• **Stratosphere:** Located above the troposphere, extending from about 15 to 50 km (9 to 31 miles) above the Earth's surface. It contains the ozone layer, which absorbs and scatters ultraviolet solar radiation.

• **Mesosphere:** The layer above the stratosphere, extending from about 50 to 80 km (31 to 50 miles) above the Earth's surface. It is known for its decreasing temperatures with altitude.

• **Thermosphere:** The layer above the mesosphere, extending from about 80 to 700 km (50 to 440 miles) above the Earth's surface. It has extremely low density and high temperatures.

• **Exosphere:** The outermost layer of the Earth's atmosphere, extending from about 700 km (440 miles) to 10,000 km (6,200 miles) above the Earth's surface. It gradually fades into the vacuum of space.

• **Meteorology:**

• Meteorology is the study of the atmosphere, including weather processes and forecasting. It involves understanding the dynamics of the atmosphere and the physical and chemical processes that occur within it.

• Meteorologists use data from weather stations, satellites, and other sources to analyze and predict weather patterns and events.
